1	# Extracting lessons from a working session
2	
3	> **Scope: a single agent ↔ user conversation.** This doc is the **method** for mining one
4	> working session's *dialogue and the actions taken in it* for improvements. It is **not** the
5	> growth extract ([the growth-extract task](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) that mines **issues, PRs, and commits** over repo
6	> history — that routine never sees a conversation. Its two callers: the
7	> [conversation-extract daily task](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md), which applies it to **captured**
8	> conversation logs — where the friction signals below (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a
9	> wait you sat through) survive with their timestamps — and an owner's occasional plain-words
10	> ask for a retrospective over the live session.
11	
12	Portable guidance for mining an agent ↔ user session — a Claude Code web session, a CLI run, a
13	captured conversation log — for durable improvements: read the conversation and convert its
14	friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less dependent on human
15	feedback.
16	
17	Run the reflection on a **capable model.** Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears
18	the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong
19	"lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
20	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model
21	to the judgment it must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the
22	separate efficiency analysis — also live there; this doc is the how-to.
23	
24	## The goal
25	
26	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less
27	rework, less waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but
28	as "where did this cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost
29	next time." If a pass can't name a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's
30	fine (see [No new lessons](#no-new-lessons-is-a-valid--and-common--result)).
31	
32	## When it runs
33	
34	Routinely, in the [conversation-extract daily task](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md) over each captured
35	log (a fresh pass within a day of capture, a final hindsight pass before retention deletes the
36	log) — the standard path. If an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective over the live
37	session, apply the same method and deliver the capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**,
38	never one that self-merges (the nightly auto-merges its own PR per its own doc; a live retrospective
39	wants human eyes). **Never
40	reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner
41	decides when a session is done enough to mine.
42	
43	## What to look for — the friction signals
44	
45	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop
46	cost more than necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
47	
48	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
49	
50	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I
51	meant…"); the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same
52	request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
53	
54	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every
55	question the user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate
56	**convention or glossary entry**; a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first
57	checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc the agent reads cold and gets right the first
58	time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds correctly **without the round-trip**.
59	
60	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
61	
62	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran
63	a command that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light
64	one fit; reinvented something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written
65	to "verify"; missed an existing convention and had it corrected in review.
66	
67	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing
68	helper/convention so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read.** Place
69	it by where the trap is hit, not in a central bucket: a gotcha from **misusing a specific API,
70	class, or library goes as a comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where
71	the next editor of that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list.
72	Co-locate it in a file's own header comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only
73	hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a central gotchas doc for what no single usage site
74	owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant file (a mistake of omission), or a
75	cross-cutting invariant. The test: next time the agent takes the good path first, not after a
76	detour.
77	
78	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
79	
80	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been
81	parallel; a padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its
82	result was already in hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already
83	green.
84	
85	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers and separate the
86	kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting** (sleeps,
87	polling, a finished process not yet killed). A captured log carries per-entry timestamps and
88	per-message token usage, so the numbers are computable, not estimated. A fix is only credible
89	against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
90	was already optimal.
91	
92	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
93	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the
94	subject of the standing **efficiency analysis** in
95	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold a wall-time
96	finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
97	loss of quality.
98	
99	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
100	
101	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks
102	*repeatedly* are a checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how
103	many processes ran — could it be fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its
104	work was done?", stop waiting to be asked — fold those exact questions into a **standing
105	self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the relevant work, and close with a
106	terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each recurring question
107	converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
108	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively,
109	with numbers.
110	
111	## From signal to lesson — the bar
112	
113	A friction signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and
114	generalizable beyond this one session.** Before adding anything:
115	
116	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded
117	  differently, even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
118	- **Route to the local pack that owns it, and prefer the strongest mechanism** — the **local
119	  promotion ladder**, at the project's own level. A project's capture surface is its **local
120	  packs** (`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/`): pick the pack whose territory the lesson belongs
121	  to, then a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in that pack's `rules` (its failure message
122	  *is* the lesson; ship it with a red-first fixture), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a
123	  **pack skill**, and only what neither can carry lands as terse **prose** in the pack's
124	  `RULES.md`. Write more checks and less prose — a check relieves every session's context
125	  completely where prose only relocates it. A gotcha tied to one call site still goes as a
126	  comment at that site (above), not into any pack. When no pack's scope fits and the lesson
127	  warrants segregation, a new local pack is a self-contained directory drop.
128	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared,
129	  cross-project canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote
130	  stage lifts it there centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever
131	  travels.
132	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or
133	  something already implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
134	
135	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
136	
137	Most sessions yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write nothing
138	rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes
139	the canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a
140	genuinely new, reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
141

1	# grow_with_claudinite
2	
3	Opt into the **growth lifecycle** — declaring this pack enrolls a repo in contributing its hard-won
4	lessons up to the shared Claudinite canon, and in pruning its local packs once the canon owns them.
5	Seeded by default (`--init` + the one-time `grow-with-claudinite-seed` baseline migration for the
6	existing fleet), and **opt-out by removal**: baselining never re-adds it.
7	
8	This pack carries the **repo-side** stages of the growth lifecycle: capturing a repo's own
9	lessons into its local packs, and pruning them once the shared canon covers them. The central
10	**promote** stage — which lifts portable lessons up into the shared canon — is a home-only duty
11	that runs canon-side, not a repo-side task, so it lives outside this pack.
12	
13	Its scheduled work is five tasks under this pack's own `tasks/`, each discovered by the repo's
14	scheduler (`engine/scheduler/discover.mjs`) wherever the pack is declared:
15	
16	| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| `growth-extract` ([tasks/growth-extract/task.md](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) | the project changed in the window | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI |
19	| `growth-dedup` ([tasks/growth-dedup/task.md](tasks/growth-dedup/task.md)) | canon changed, or the project's local packs changed (or weekly) | a PR against the repo's `main` |
20	| `growth-discover-packs` ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) | weekly | a new **local** pack in the repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`, via a reviewed PR |
21	| `conversation-extract` ([tasks/conversation-extract/task.md](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md)) | after a substantive merge, or to run the retention prune | the repo's own local packs, plus the prune on the logs branch |
22	| `prose-to-checks-sweep` ([tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md](tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)) | daily (no-ops cheaply on a quiet corpus) | a PR converting always-testable pack prose into checks |
23	
24	A member that wants the local stages without contributing lessons upstream **opts out of
25	promotion** on its own entry — `{ "id": "grow_with_claudinite", "config": { "promote": false } }`
26	— and the central promote stage skips it (absent or `true` = participate).
27	
28	## The conversation lifecycle — capture in-session, extract in a daily task, retention
29	
30	The pack also owns **extraction from working sessions** — the conversation-side sibling of the
31	issues/PRs/commits extract above, replacing the old in-session post-merge lessons pass. The two
32	halves split by what each needs: **capture** needs the live session transcript, so it runs
33	in-session (at merge, and again when the session ends); **extraction** only reads the
34	already-pushed logs, so it is an ordinary
35	scheduled task with `growth-extract`'s access model — the logs branch is *in the repo*,
36	so reading it, committing lessons to local packs, and pruning are plain local git on the working
37	tree; only posting the summary on the issue uses the GitHub MCP tools.
38	
39	1. **Capture — a step in the merge-to-main skill** (in-session, where the transcript lives).
40	   Right after a merge lands:
41	   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
42	   (in the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`).
43	   Deterministic, seconds; it bundles the session transcript (sidechains inline, timestamp
44	   order), **scrubs enumeration-first** (every value the environment holds — `process.env`
45	   minus a short named allowlist of structural values, plus known credential stores — is
46	   redacted wherever it appears, with credential-shape patterns as the backstop; a secret the
47	   session itself transformed is beyond any static scrub, and push protection is the last
48	   net), and pushes one file per **capture event** onto the orphan **`conversation-logs`**
49	   branch: `<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`, commits marked `[skip ci]`.
50	   **Delta-aware, keyed on the session id:** every capture pushes only the entries after this
51	   session's previous capture, whatever event produced it, so any two events chain into
52	   disjoint files and a zero delta pushes nothing at all. Double-writing is therefore safe by
53	   construction, not by coordination — the property [`session-end.mjs`](session-end.mjs) relies
54	   on, so `pack.test.mjs` pins it directly.
55	   The branch is a **work queue, not an archive** — never merged; tips are cheap in shallow
56	   session clones and retention keeps them bounded.
57	1. **Capture — again, when the session ends** ([session-end.mjs](session-end.mjs), invoked by the
58	   engine's SessionEnd hook runner for every active pack that ships one). Same capture, with
59	   `--issue 0`: **`0` means "no associated issue"**, and the filename shape stays byte-identical
60	   on purpose — the retention prune, the `conversationLogs` signal and the extract's filename
61	   parse all already accept it, whereas a *new* shape would be invisible to the prune and become
62	   immortal on the branch. This event is what captures the sessions that never merge (a review, an
63	   investigation, a session that ended in a question) and the post-merge **tail** of the ones that
64	   do. **Best effort:** a container reclaimed by timeout never fires it, so nothing depends on it
65	   having run — every firing enriches the record, every miss leaves exactly the merge-only
66	   behaviour. An `issue-0` log has no issue for `conversation-extract` to post its exchange
67	   summary on; nothing else about its lifecycle differs.
68	2. **Fresh pass — the [conversation-extract](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md) scheduled task**
69	   (precondition: a substantive merge, or a logs branch with retention configured so the age-based
70	   prune still runs on a quiet repo; local git on the
71	   repo's working tree, MCP only for the issue comment). It applies
72	   [extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md) (the method — friction signals and the
73	   measured efficiency analysis, computable from the log's timestamps and token usage), routes
74	   keepers into the member's local packs, and posts on the worked issue, for each rule that landed,
75	   a **200-word-max** summary of the slice of conversation that caused it — the dialogue itself is
76	   never pasted there, it is far too verbose for an issue —
77	   **extraction is the only path to permanence**: a log that yields no rule gets no comment,
78	   and its conversation is gone once retention deletes it (a deliberate owner call).
79	3. **Final pass and deletion** — once a log ages past `config.retention_days`, the same task
80	   re-reads it with ~a week of hindsight (the rethink window), then deletes it (the weekly full
81	   sweep guarantees the prune runs even on a repo gone quiet). Every log gets exactly two
82	   judgment passes. **Unset retention = the prune deletes nothing** (capture-only, fail-safe).
83	
84	No adoption question over it — `retention_days` stays unset (hidden) by default, which is
85	fail-safe (capture-only). A project that wants the prune active sets `config.retention_days`
86	itself (10 is the recommended floor); nothing else to schedule, since extraction rides the
87	fleet's one daily run like the other growth tasks.
88	
89	## Skill-usage metrics — what the mounted skills actually do
90	
91	Mounting a skill only puts its name and one-line description into the session prompt; whether the
92	model ever **loads** it is discretion, and nothing recorded it. So the promotion ladder's
93	skill-vs-prose call had no empirical feedback: a skill whose trigger never fires looked exactly like
94	one that fires daily, and a "skill" that loads in every session (rules wearing a skill's clothes)
95	looked exactly like a genuinely activity-scoped one.
96	
97	The [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/task.md) task closes that loop — daily, agentless, seconds. It
98	counts skill loads **and their denominators** (captures, merges, sessions, user messages, user
99	commands) out of the logs this pack already captures, into
100	`.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`: day rows recomputed statelessly inside the raw retention
101	window, week rows appended once past a `foldedThrough` watermark. Denominators are the point — a raw
102	count cannot tell healthy-rare from broken, so the question is loads *against the sessions where that
103	skill's own declared trigger plausibly applied*. Zeros are implicit (a skill with no loads has no
104	key), which is what makes "never loads" visible: diff the file against the repo's mounted skills.
105	
106	Fleet-wide aggregation is deliberately **not** here — the canon knows mechanisms, never repos. It is
107	the sheepdog pack's [`fleet-usage`](../sheepdog/tasks/fleet-usage/task.md) task, in the fleet-enforcer
108	repo, which is the only place that knows who the members are.
109	
110	## Rules
111	
112	| Rule | Kind | What |
113	|---|---|---|
114	| `growth-config` | hardcoded ([config-check.mjs](config-check.mjs)) | entry config shape valid |
115	
116	**Pack discovery** ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) is
117	an ordinary weekly task on the repo's own scheduler. The repo runs the whole pipeline over
118	**itself**: manifest its stack, hold it against the canon packs already on its shelf and its own
119	existing local packs, and — for genuinely project-specific knowledge neither homes — author a new
120	**local** pack populated from its real usage, landed through a **reviewed** PR (a new pack ships new
121	`.mjs` checks, and a check can break CI — the same reason `prose-to-checks-sweep` is reviewed, and
122	the one place this stage differs from extract). It writes only the repo's own
123	`.claudinite/local/packs/`; lifting a local pack up into the shared canon is the central promote
124	task's job.
125	
126	## Identifying a project's capture surface: its local packs (the same way in every stage)
127	
128	Every growth stage operates on a project's **local packs** — the tracked packs a repo keeps under
129	`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` (prose in `RULES.md`, checks in the pack's `rules`, activity
130	procedures as the pack's skills, scheduled tasks under its `tasks/`). That subtree **is** the
131	project's own content;
132	the rest of `.claudinite/` is the **read-only mounted canon** and is never a capture, prune, or
133	promote target. So "a project's local packs" means precisely *everything under
134	`.claudinite/local_packs/`, and nothing else under `.claudinite/`*. This is the normalized capture
135	surface — a structural set the stages read the same way, not a `CLAUDE.md`-graph walk over stray
136	Markdown (a repo with no local packs yet simply has nothing to extract, dedup, or promote here; a
137	project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill).
138	
139	Prefer the strongest mechanism the lesson allows — the **local promotion ladder**, applied at the
140	project's own level: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in the owning pack's `rules` (its
141	failure message carries the lesson), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack skill**, and only
142	what neither can carry lands as **prose** in a pack's `RULES.md`. A check relieves every session's
143	context completely where prose only relocates it, so capture writes *more checks and less prose*.
144	
145	The stages differ only in *how they read that set*, never in *which set it is*: extract and dedup
146	run against the member repo and read the local packs from the working tree; promote runs centrally
147	and reads the same subtree over the GitHub API (get-file-contents under `.claudinite/local_packs/`).
148	Extract writes into it, promote reads from it, dedup prunes within it — all against the identical,
149	`.claudinite/local_packs/`-rooted set.
150

1	---
2	name: generate-project-instructions
3	description: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
4	---
5	
6	# Generate project instructions — extract packs, not a project doc
7	
8	This skill grows the corpus's pack library using the project in front of you as the evidence, and
9	lands the project's own working rules where every project's do now: its **local packs**. The owner's
10	projects recur — not as wholes, but **along axes**: the same working style returns with a different
11	product, the same technology returns with a different working style, the same audience returns on a
12	different stack. The first project to exhibit a facet pays the cost of working out how that facet is
13	handled; a **canon** pack is how every later project sharing it starts from the answer instead of
14	re-deriving it — and what stays specific to *this* project lands in **its own local pack**, the same
15	pack machinery run from the project's tree.
16	
17	The deliverable is therefore **two kinds of pack**, never a single "how to work on this repo" document:
18	
19	- **Canon pack seeds and refinements** — one `packs/<facet>/` per facet where this project has real
20	  portable insight, each written as if this project didn't exist, proposed to Claudinite.
21	- **The project's own local pack(s)** — under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the project's tree:
22	  the project-specific working style, concrete values (real commands, paths, names, metrics), and the
23	  project-specific rules that *don't* generalize — carried the same way any pack carries them (a check
24	  in the pack's `rules`, an activity skill, prose in `RULES.md`, a scheduled task), not a thin doc.
25	  This is the project's normalized capture surface; its `CLAUDE.md` is a thin routing map to it, loaded
26	  through the pack system rather than `@import`.
27	
28	The failure mode this skill exists to prevent: investigating the repo and producing one competent "how
29	to work on this repo" document — real commands, real paths, this product's concepts — with the
30	reusable core never separated out and the project-specific core dumped as always-loaded prose. If
31	portable guidance ends up in a local pack (it should be a canon pack), or the project's file names end
32	up in a canon pack (they belong in the local pack), the split is wrong.
33	
34	## 1. Gather the evidence
35	
36	Read the project before writing a word: README and existing docs, `CLAUDE.md` and everything it
37	imports, dependency and build manifests, scripts and CI, the test layout, git history and recent
38	PRs/issues, and any conversation with the owner about how they want to work. You are collecting two
39	things, both grounded in what you actually find:
40	
41	- the **facets** this project exhibits (step 2), and
42	- every **candidate rule** — each convention, procedure, or quality bar the project works by — ready to
43	  be sorted by owner (step 3).
44	
45	Invent nothing. If a call that changes the outcome is genuinely open, ask the owner one focused
46	question (via the structured popup); otherwise take the sensible default and note it.
47	
48	## 2. Decompose into facets, and check the shelf per facet
49	
50	A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:
51	
52	- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
53	  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
54	  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.
55	- **Technology — the platform.** True for any project on that platform, whatever its class or product.
56	  Test: the pack still fits when the product and the working style change. The first project on a new
57	  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way
58	  `chrome-extension` and `aws-sam` were minted.
59	- **Aspect — a separable slice of concern**, usually with its own on-switch. `chrome-extension-release`
60	  is the same technology as `chrome-extension` at a different moment: the release/store standard a
61	  project declares only once it ships. Split an aspect out of its parent facet when its rules activate
62	  at a different time or under a different decision than the parent's.
63	- **Domain — the audience or setting**, when it changes how work is done. A children's-app pack would
64	  carry design-review, requirement-processing, and compliance rules that hold whether the app is
65	  Flutter or web; a regulated-industry pack likewise. A domain that doesn't change the working rules
66	  isn't a facet worth a pack.
67	
68	**The product itself is never a facet** — "this specific product" doesn't recur, by definition; its
69	rules land in the project's own local pack.
70	
71	And a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon
72	or local, homes **how we work**: the conventions, gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks
73	whatever the feature happens to be. A rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or
74	that a feature's parts are wired to each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable
75	spec and the suite that proves it. Encoding it as a pack check instead splits one feature's definition
76	across two systems and lands it in the one no test of the product ever reads. Pack-worthiness is a question
77	about the *work*, not about how load-bearing the code is — a real gap in product coverage is a requirements
78	gap, and answering it with a pack is how a feature's spec ends up somewhere nothing executes it.
79	
80	<example>
81	One extension project can exhibit four facets at once: `spec-driven-product` (class),
82	`chrome-extension` + `node` (technologies), `chrome-extension-release` (aspect, once it ships) — and
83	its local pack holds only what none of them own.
84	</example>
85	
86	Then check the canon shelf **per facet** (`packs/` here; the mounted `.claudinite/packs/` in a
87	consuming repo — a facet already owned by a *canon* pack is declared, not re-authored locally):
88	
89	- **Covered** → declare it (technology facets are usually already declared from the fingerprint) and
90	  move on — unless this project's evidence **sharpens or contradicts** the pack, which becomes a
91	  refinement PR to that pack, not a fork. Each further project of a facet is another exemplar: the
92	  pack should read as the intersection-plus-union of all of them, and a rule only one exemplar
93	  supports should say so or wait.
94	- **Uncovered, with real portable insight in the evidence** → this skill mints it (steps 3–4).
95	- **Uncovered, but this project has nothing durable to say about it yet** → leave it; a pack of
96	  placeholders helps nobody.
97	
98	Write each facet down — a short name plus one defining sentence — before drafting anything; every
99	sorting decision in step 3 tests against them.
100	
101	## 3. Sort every candidate rule to the single facet that owns it
102	
103	For each rule from step 1, apply the **portability strip per facet**: delete from the rule everything
104	the facet doesn't keep, and see whether something meaningful survives.
105	
106	- Delete the product and the stack, keep the loop — survives? → the **class** pack (canon).
107	- Delete the product and the working style, keep the platform — survives? → the **technology** (or
108	  **aspect**) pack (canon).
109	- Delete the stack, keep the audience/setting — survives? → the **domain** pack (canon).
110	- Survives nothing → project-specific: the project's **own local pack**.
111	
112	Route each rule to **exactly one owner** — the facet whose whole population the rule serves. "True for
113	any Node service" belongs to the canon `node` pack, not to this project's class pack, even if every
114	project of the class happens to use Node. Rewrite what lands in a canon pack project-agnostically and
115	parameterized, the way research-project does ("read *input* as whatever it means for your project").
116	
117	Then gate **every** pack-bound rule — canon or local — on the promotion ladder
118	([engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md)): a rule a deterministic **check** could enforce, or a
119	procedure with a nameable trigger a **skill** could carry, becomes that (in a canon seed it's flagged
120	as a check/skill candidate; in a local pack you author the check outright in the pack's `rules`, with
121	a red-first fixture) rather than settling as prose. What remains in a `RULES.md` is the always-relevant
122	judgment core of its facet — write more checks and less prose. Dedupe against the corpus: a rule the
123	basics baseline, an existing canon pack, or a skill already owns is not pack material at all.
124	
125	## 4. Write each pack
126	
127	Mint a pack for a facet only when its surviving rules clear the bar — several durable rules, not one
128	stray (a single rule joins the nearest existing pack, or waits as a handoff note). Each
129	`packs/<facet>/` needs four things (mirror `research-project/` and `chrome-extension/`):
130	
131	- **`RULES.md`** — the playbook, addressed to the *next* project sharing the facet, on day one. Open
132	  with the facet's one-line definition and "a default to adapt, not a contract". Principle-first, each
133	  rule carrying its why. It loads at session start for every declaring project, so every line pays
134	  rent — cover the facet, not everything you noticed.
135	- **`pack.mjs`** — the manifest. Class/domain/aspect packs: `always: false`, `marker: null`,
136	  `detect: null` (declaration is authoritative). Technology packs: add the `marker`/`detect`
137	  fingerprint when the repo carries a reliable one, so `--init` seeds the pack into a fresh
138	  declaration; the marker only *suspects* a pack is wanted, it never forces its declaration.
139	  Discovery is structural — the directory is the registration.
140	- **`README.md`** — the pack's rule table (section ≤5 words | how enforced), plus one provenance line
141	  naming the project it was distilled from.
142	- **Index entries** — a row in [packs/README.md](../../../../packs/README.md) and, for a new pack kind, the
143	  matching line in the corpus map ([README.md](../../../../README.md) — there is no agent-facing corpus index, #385).
144	
145	The acid test before proposing any pack: **a reader must not be able to tell which project it was
146	extracted from.** Any surviving repo path, command line, or product noun marks a rule that belonged in
147	the overlay.
148	
149	## 5. Write the project's own local pack(s)
150	
151	The project-specific residue lands in a **local pack** under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the
152	project's tree — the same pack machinery, run from the project instead of the canon. Most projects
153	need **one** general pack (name it for the project); segregate a **second** only when a distinct domain
154	earns its own bundle (the way the reference project split a general working pack from an
155	extractor-automation pack). Each local pack is a real pack:
156	
157	- **`pack.mjs`** — `{ id, detect: null, marker: null, prose: 'RULES.md', rules: [...], skills: [...] }`.
158	  A local pack is declared by hand, never fingerprinted or seeded (`detect`/`marker` stay null), as its
159	  namespaced token `local_packs/<name>` in `.claudinite-checks.json`; its id
160	  must be unique and may not shadow a canon pack.
161	- **`RULES.md`** — the always-loaded judgment core and the project's concrete values (real
162	  setup/run/verify commands, real paths, inputs, metrics, invariants). Keep it terse; anything a check
163	  or skill can carry doesn't belong here, and anything inferable from the code is omitted.
164	- **Checks** (`rules`) — the project-specific deterministic rules as `.mjs` modules listed on
165	  `pack.mjs`, each with a red-first fixture (`pack.test.mjs`) runnable by the project's own test suite.
166	  Local check modules stay dependency-free (they must load without the gitignored mount): return plain
167	  finding objects rather than importing the engine's helpers.
168	- **Skills** (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — the project's activity-scoped procedures, bundled in the pack;
169	  a local pack may also *require* a canon skill by name.
170	- **Scheduled tasks** (`tasks/<name>/task.mjs` + its `task.md`) — first-class like every other slot:
171	  the repo's own scheduler discovers a local pack's tasks in the same scan that finds a canon pack's,
172	  gated by the project's declaration exactly the same way. So project-specific scheduled work belongs
173	  in a local task declaration (a self-contained module honoring the task contract, with its
174	  co-located worker doc), not an out-of-repo routine and not a cron of its own.
175	
176	The project's `CLAUDE.md` becomes a thin **routing map** to its local packs (and its genuine design
177	docs) — it does **not** `@import` the pack prose; the pack system injects the active local packs'
178	`RULES.md` at session start, the same as the canon packs'.
179	
180	## 6. Deliver through the owner's approval gates
181	
182	- **Every canon pack seed or refinement → a PR against Claudinite.** Minting or changing a *canon* pack
183	  is the owner's call, and the PR is that gate — no corpus change lands unattended
184	  ([the canon-curation README](../../../../.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/README.md)). From a consuming repo, never edit the read-only
185	  `.claudinite/` mount: open the Claudinite PR when the session can reach that repo; otherwise stage the
186	  seed as a **local pack** clearly marked as a proposed-canon facet and open a Claudinite issue pointing
187	  at it, so the promote stage lifts it centrally.
188	- **The project's local pack(s) → the project's normal branch/PR**, committed under
189	  `.claudinite/local_packs/` (tracked project content — the sync hook preserves it, the gitignore
190	  re-includes it). Declaring a **local** pack — as `local_packs/<name>` — is valid immediately (the
191	  engine discovers local packs from the repo), so the declaration lands in the same PR.
192	- **Declare a new *canon* pack** in `.claudinite-checks.json` only after it has merged and the mount
193	  re-synced — declaring a canon id the mounted registry doesn't know is an unknown-pack settings error;
194	  a *local* id is never that error. Note a pending canon declaration as a follow-up in the project PR.
195	- **Existing projects sharing a facet keep their local packs for now.** Once the canon pack lands, the
196	  growth dedup stage prunes what the canon newly owns; don't pre-trim against an unmerged pack.
197	
198	Close with a short report: each facet and its one-line definition, with its shelf verdict (declared /
199	refined / minted-to-canon / kept-local / left alone); the sort tally (rules sent to each canon pack /
200	the local pack / as a check vs. a skill vs. prose); and links to the PRs.
201

1	# Executable requirements — the framework standard
2	
3	The concrete conventions for running a numbered spec as tests. The judgment layer — doc-first
4	red-by-default, owner-owned expecteds, honest-gap tracking — is the
5	[spec-driven-product](../spec-driven-product/RULES.md) playbook; this pack is the mechanics that
6	implement it, so a new project or a new stack adopts the framework by convention instead of
7	re-deriving it. Worked implementations: GoogleCalendarEventCreator (origin; extension/jsdom
8	rendering), TLDR (adds a cross-tier `server` kind), ShoutsAndWhispers (Flutter port; first `saga`
9	kind).
10	
11	## 1. The layout is the contract
12	
13	- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
14	  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
15	  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
16	- **A requirement line** starts (optionally after a list dash) with a backtick-wrapped dotted
17	  number: `` `4.2` ``. A **leaf** is an id with no finer-numbered child. Parse with one shared
18	  regex (`` ^\s*(?:-\s+)?`(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)` ``) so specs stay drop-in compatible across projects.
19	- **The line is a scannable one-liner; expanded detail collapses.** A leaf in `requirements.md`
20	  reads as a single line the owner skims down the numbered spine on GitHub. Any expansion —
21	  rationale, acceptance notes, edge cases, the owner-verification recipe — lives inside a
22	  collapsed `<details>` block under the line, hidden until the owner expands it. The doc reviews
23	  as a clean spec, not walls of prose; the depth is one click away when wanted, invisible when
24	  not.
25	- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; the case declares no
26	  kind field. Cases are
27	  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
28	  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id.
29	- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
30	  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
31	- Where the language discovers cases dynamically (Node `require`), the registry walks the
32	  folders; where it cannot (Dart/Flutter), each kind keeps a hand-written `manifest` and **the
33	  gate enforces manifest ⇄ disk equality** — an unregistered case file never runs, so unregistered
34	  must be red.
35	
36	## 2. What the coverage gate checks
37	
38	The bijection gate is one committed test. It must fail on every one of: a leaf no case claims
39	(doc-first red-by-default); a case claiming a non-existent leaf; two cases claiming one leaf; a misnamed case file; a kind directory absent from the registry (or a
40	registered kind with no directory); a manifest out of sync with disk (where manifests exist); an
41	image found in a coded kind's folder (a screenshot cannot verify a gesture or a pure rule); a
42	stray golden no case or step accounts for. Every rule iterates the registry — adding a kind never
43	edits the gate.
44	
45	The gate checks repo state; an interactive feature run also has an *ordering*: after the
46	owner's feature-classified comment, an independent commit updating the spec (no code alongside)
47	precedes the first code commit on the branch. The spec's path defaults to the canonical
48	`dev/requirements/requirements.md`; a project whose spec lives elsewhere (a non-canonical
49	layout, or the pack pulled in via a `requires` from `spec-driven-product`) names it on the pack
50	entry as `config.spec`.
51	
52	## 3. The kind vocabulary
53	
54	Two forces pick a leaf's kind: what can **honestly observe** the assertion, and what gives the
55	**owner the simplest verification**. Prefer the kind whose expected is a **visual the owner checks
56	by sight** — a surface snapshot or a saga storyboard — and whose per-leaf test body is minimal:
57	drive to the state, capture, done, with the golden as the assertion rather than hand-written
58	expectations. Push as many requirements as can honestly be seen onto that visual path — the more
59	of the spec an owner verifies by *looking*, the more of it they actually review. Reserve the coded
60	kinds (behavior, logic) for what an image genuinely cannot see: a gesture's outgoing request, a
61	pure rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually see what it asserts:
62	
63	- **surface snapshot** (`popup`, `icon`, `screen`, …): a rendered resting state, pixel-exact
64	  against a committed golden. One golden per leaf, even when several leaves render the same state
65	  — the bijection stays strict.
66	- **behavior**: a driven gesture and its outgoing request/consequence, asserted in code against
67	  the fakes' recordings. No images allowed in the folder.
68	- **logic**: a pure product rule, a coded `verify()` importing shipped code.
69	- **saga** (§4): a multi-step story as a golden storyboard.
70	- **per-project kinds** where the product's value is breadth or crosses tiers: a per-target
71	  `extractor`/`support` kind (one case per supported external target, proven on committed real
72	  samples), a `server` kind (the boundary's half of a two-tier rule, against the real handler).
73	- **heavy/e2e singleton**: "the product loads in the real environment" — one case, its own lane,
74	  never in the default loop.
75	
76	## 4. Sagas: stories as storyboards
77	
78	Single frames prove states; **sagas prove transitions and causality** — what arriving, acting, or
79	time passing *changes*. Use a saga when the requirement is the story ("a message sent before I
80	arrived never appears; one sent after I arrived does"), not decomposable into independent resting
81	states without losing the claim.
82	
83	- A saga case is an ordered list of **steps**; each step = a caption plus an action against the
84	  fake world; after each step the runner captures one golden frame `<slug>.<id>.step-NN.png`.
85	- The **caption narrates the story** in user terms — captions surface in the gallery.
86	- One saga = one leaf; the frames are that one case's expected (all frames pixel-exact, same
87	  ownership rules as any golden). Keep sagas to 3–6 frames; a longer story is usually two sagas.
88	- Saga steps drive the **same real entry point** as every other kind (the shipped app shell/render
89	  function) — a saga must never become a scripted slideshow of hand-arranged states.
90	
91	**Animated saga goldens** (recording the motion, not the frames). A per-step frame proves a resting
92	state; a saga can instead be **one animated golden** — an APNG per leaf — recording the real UI
93	*moving* between steps. What keeps it delay-free and deterministic:
94	
95	- **Strip dead delay, keep the animation.** Render time is virtual, so a scripted wait is a run of
96	  *identical* frames — dedup consecutive identical frames and clamp any single hold, so the golden
97	  holds motion, never waiting (a 3 s wait must not become 3 s of golden).
98	- **Lossless, so byte-identity still holds.** Encode APNG, not GIF (whose palette and dithering
99	  aren't deterministic); the comparison stays exact byte-identity and a mismatch writes a per-frame
100	  `expected | actual | diff` to the gitignored failures dir. Capture at a low DPR — lossless costs
101	  no fidelity for it. Flutter reads each frame off the `RepaintBoundary` via `toImage` inside
102	  `runAsync` (the fake-async test zone won't otherwise complete the byte read).
103	- **Mark the gesture.** Paint an expanding ring at each real pointer gesture over the pre-reaction
104	  frame so the strip shows *where* the user acted; programmatic world changes draw none.
105	
106	## 5. Determinism or it isn't spec
107	
108	A rendered expected is only owner-ownable if it is byte-stable forever:
109	
110	- **Pin the clock.** One shared reference time (`REFERENCE_NOW`) threaded to everything that
111	  formats or compares dates; fixture data is authored relative to it. Never wall-clock.
112	- **Fake every nondeterministic input**: network (map tiles, avatars — deterministic generated
113	  substitutes), randomness, platform sensors, locale (pin it; date copy is locale-sensitive),
114	  viewport (one fixed logical size and pixel ratio).
115	- **Load real fonts** in the render harness — test environments default to a glyph-less stub that
116	  renders text as boxes. Load the product's bundled families plus the
117	  icon font; watch for styles that don't inherit the family (button text styles are the classic
118	  leak) — pin the family there explicitly.
119	- **Never wait for "settled".** Indeterminate spinners animate forever; use fixed-duration pumps
120	  so an in-flight state is a capturable, deterministic frame.
121	
122	## 6. Rendering recipes per stack
123	
124	- **Browser-extension / DOM products** (the origin recipe): feed the case's fake data to the real
125	  `render()` in a jsdom document seeded from the real HTML, fold the real CSS on as inline styles,
126	  rasterize with satori + resvg, compare with pixelmatch at **zero tolerated diff ratio**. No real
127	  browser: deterministic and dependency-light, at a documented fidelity tradeoff.
128	- **Flutter**: widget-test golden files are the native equivalent — pump the real app shell
129	  against the fake world and `matchesGoldenFile`; `--update-goldens` is the refresh lane. Load
130	  fonts from the FontManifest (icons included). The fake world (scripted location/auth/backend
131	  that also *records* what the UI asked) is the product's own testing library so the requirements
132	  package and unit tests share it.
133	- Whatever the stack: the comparison is **pixel-exact**. A tolerance is a standing invitation for
134	  unreviewed drift; if a platform renders unstably, fix the determinism (fonts, clock, fakes), not
135	  the threshold.
136	
137	## 7. The gallery is derived output
138	
139	- The spec doubles as a visual gallery: under every image-kind leaf, machine-managed image lines
140	  (tagged with an HTML comment marker) embed the committed goldens — saga leaves get their full
141	  captioned storyboard strip.
142	- A committed **gallery gate** keeps the doc equal to the generator's output byte-for-byte.
143	  Regenerate via the tool, never by hand.
144	
145	## 8. Refresh is a review step
146	
147	One committed refresh entry point regenerates all goldens **and** the gallery together, so they
148	cannot skew. Running it is how an *intended* UI change lands — the refreshed PNGs ride the diff
149	for the owner to approve. It is never how a red case gets fixed: the re-baselining approval
150	procedure (surface actual/expected/diff, ask, only then re-baseline) is canon in the
151	writing-tests skill and the spec-driven-product playbook.

=== growth-discover-packs task.md 35-50 ===

### 2. Find the gap — what is pack-worthy but unhomed

Now hold the manifest against two things: the **available canon packs** (`.claudinite/shared/packs/`) and the repo's **existing local packs**. A candidate for a new **local** pack is a technology or domain that:

- the repo genuinely uses (not `vestigial`), and carries real, reusable working knowledge for — a build/config gotcha, a domain rule, a project-specific procedure that recurs; **and**
- **no canon pack already homes** — a technology is **homed**, so drop it, when any pack owns it, **a stub pack included** (if the canon covers it, the repo should just *declare that canon pack*, not re-create it locally — note that as the action instead); **and**
- the repo's **existing local packs don't already capture** (if a local pack owns that territory, a new rule belongs in it — that's [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md)'s job, not a new pack).

What remains is project-specific knowledge that deserves its own local pack: a domain the project works in, or a technology the canon doesn't home, with enough captured knowledge to justify a pack rather than a loose rule.

### 3. Author the local pack — distilled from the repo's real usage

For each candidate, author a populated pack under `.claudinite/local/packs/<name>/`, distilled from **how this project actually works** — never from imagination. Apply the [generate-project-instructions](../../skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) method (don't re-derive it): descend the promotion ladder ([engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md)) — a rule a deterministic check can carry becomes the **check plus a see-it-fail fixture** (fires on a violating input, quiet on a clean one), a procedure with a nameable trigger becomes a skill, and only signature-less judgment lands as `RULES.md` prose. Ground and cite every rule in the project's real files. **Never pad** with speculative best-practice rules the evidence doesn't demonstrate; a rule you can't ground, you don't write — a smaller honest pack beats a padded one. And **never open an empty stub to fill later**. Write the pack files (`RULES.md`, `pack.mjs`, `README.md`), register it, and **declare it** in the repo's `.claudinite-checks.json` so it actually activates.

### 4. Open the PR for review

Land the new pack (and its declaration) through a single PR on a per-run-unique branch (see [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)) — title `Claudinite growth: discover local pack <name>`, and **put the issue reference in the commit message**: `Refs #<n>` for this task's tracking issue (below), in the commit itself, not only the PR body, so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. **Never arm auto-merge** — the reviewer is the point. A new check must still ship green (see it fail on a violating fixture, pass on a clean one) so CI stays green and the reviewer has something mergeable; a rule that can't be made a confident check lands as prose instead.

## How it finds lessons (scoped to the window in Context)

1. **Read the window.** The window's **commits** (the shas named in Context — full bodies, diffs where a fix is non-obvious) and the **issue/PR activity** it names (the changed comments on those numbers). Where Context names PRs **merged in the window**, read those first and read them properly — the diff *and* the review discussion. A merged PR is usually the window's richest lesson source: it records what was tried, what a reviewer pushed back on, and why the landed shape won.
2. **Extract only durable, reusable lessons** — gotchas, engineering practices, test discipline, architecture rules, project mechanics — and **dedupe** each against what the repo already documents. When in doubt, leave it out. **An already-settled, already-enforced implementation choice is not a lesson.** If a check or test already pins the shape (which roots CI sweeps, which contract a construction must satisfy) and all that's left to say is *why it looks like that*, that explanation belongs as a comment at the implementation site — not as portable prose here, and this task has no way to place it there anyway (it writes only local packs, never the code the lesson is about). A rule earns its place by steering a **future** decision or catching a **repeatable** mistake, not by narrating a past one that's already locked in.
3. **Route each lesson to the owning local pack, and prefer the strongest mechanism.** Pick the pack whose territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then run the **local promotion ladder**: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in that pack's `rules` (author the `.mjs`, list it on `pack.mjs`, add a red-first fixture — its failure message *is* the lesson), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack skill**, and only what neither can carry lands as terse **prose** in the pack's `RULES.md`. A gotcha tied to one call site still goes as a comment right at that site (the file-local rule — [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) owns the usage-site-vs-central call). Write more checks and less prose; keep each addition terse and in the repo's own voice.

If an edit touches something a test reads (a doc constant, a code path), run the repo's offline test suite and keep it green before opening the PR.

---

## 1. The executable spec is the backbone

- **One numbered requirements document states what the product must do**, leaf by leaf: what each
  surface must render, how it must behave, the exact copy and semantics it must carry. Not prose
  aspirations — specific, testable statements.
- **Keep the spec's boundary crisp: a leaf is what the harness can assert.** The feature-level story —
  what the product does and why — lives in the product's prose docs; the spec holds the specific,
  testable statements (exact strings, placement, semantics). A statement no kind can prove isn't a
  leaf yet: it stays prose, or it's the trigger to add the kind that can prove it.
- **Every leaf carries a stable id.** Add new requirements under new numbers; never renumber or reuse
  a retired one — the ids are what cases, commits, and review discussion key on.
- **Doc-first, red by default.** Adding a leaf with no executable proof fails the build until a case
  claims it.
- **The spec drives the tests, never the other way around.** A behavior change starts by editing the
  leaf, watching the gate go red, then changing product and proof to match. A test changed without its
  leaf — or a leaf reworded to match what the code happens to do — inverts the authority.

## 2. Every leaf ⇄ exactly one proof, of the right kind

- **Enforce the bijection with a committed coverage gate**: each leaf claimed by exactly one case,
  each case claiming exactly one leaf, and every discovered kind of case actually executed by a
  runner. The gate is part of the project's own suite.
- **A *kind* is one way a requirement can be asserted** — a rendered-state snapshot, a driven gesture,
  a pure rule, a boundary-enforced rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually observe what it
  asserts. Keep kinds **extensible** — adding one is a self-contained drop.
- **A kind may be a singleton.** "The product loads in the real environment" is a perfectly good leaf
  whose mechanism is one end-to-end case; the kind names the *way of asserting*, not a population of
  cases.
- **Give each kind's runner a named lane, and keep the default lane fast and deterministic.** Heavy
  real-environment kinds gate the merge from CI without slowing the inner loop; their trust rules
  (twice-green before merging, self-diagnosing on failure) are canon in the writing-tests skill.
- **Actuals come from the real code.** Whatever the kind, the proof drives the shipped entry points
  under a faithful harness — never a parallel re-implementation of what production "should" do (the
  writing-tests skill owns the general rule).
=== basics/README.md ===
# basics pack

The baseline pack — the `RULES.md` prose every session loads (injected by the pack-prose hook) plus the core checks. Declared explicitly like every other pack — no pack is active by default; bootstrap seeds the declaration and the nightly baselining backfills it into existing consumers.

## Checks (hardcoded)

| Check | Enforces (≤5 words) | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| `reference-integrity` | links resolve; no deleted-path references | blocking |
| `markdown-link-labels` | link label matches its target | blocking |
| `task-lifecycle` | branch commits reference an issue | blocking |
| `warning-suppression` | suppressions carry a reason on-site | blocking |
| `skill-ownership` | every skill required by some pack | blocking |
| `shared-constants` | declared copies match their count | blocking |
| `squash-merge-history` | change introduces no merge commits | blocking |
| `scheduler-workflow-shape` | scheduler workflow is thin shim | blocking |
| `task-declaration-shape` | task.mjs carries full contract | blocking |
| `file-placement` | code references stay near | advisory |
| `claude-md-length` | root CLAUDE.md under ~200 lines | advisory |
| `generated-merge-driver` | GENERATED files get merge=ours | advisory |

## Prose (`RULES.md`)

| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
|---|---|

=== prose-to-checks-sweep task.md ===
# Prose-to-checks — sweep this repo's pack prose

Mine the **existing** prose of this repo's packs — each pack's `RULES.md` / `SKILL.md` — for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Where [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) descends the ladder for each *new* lesson, this task works the *backlog*: standing prose that was always mechanizable but never converted.

You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to sweep. Work only those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. **Never** edit a read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.

The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: convert prose to checks in a single owner-approved PR (a check can break CI or misfire, so it is reviewed, not auto-merged).

## The method lives in the skill

The conversion method — how to spot an always-testable rule in prose, judge convertibility, author the check plus its **see-it-fail** fixture, and decide what stays prose — is owned by the [**prose-to-checks** skill](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker only frames the unattended run around it.

## What a run does

1. **Pick convertible prose** under the Context's pack paths — rules that are *always testable* (a deterministic condition a check could assert) and that no existing check already covers. Prefer the strongest, clearest candidates; converting one or two solid rules well beats churning many shakily.
2. **Convert per the skill** — author the rule module in its owning pack, register it in that pack's `pack.mjs`, and add a **fixture test that fires on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one** (see-it-fail is mandatory — a check that can't be made confident is left as prose, never shipped broken). Trim the now-redundant prose to rationale.
3. **Open a PR** — one PR for the run's conversions on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. Keep the repo's offline test suite green before opening.
4. **Log to the tracker** — the standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks`** in this repo. Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing. **Never open, close, or reopen it**. Log each run as a **dated comment**: the prose converted and the check id it became, or "nothing convertible this run".

## What this task must never do

- **Never ship a check that can't be made confident** — the see-it-fail fixture is the gate; an unprovable rule stays prose.
- **Never convert a rule an existing check already covers** — dedupe against the check set first.
- **Never touch a pack path outside the Context**, and **never edit a mounted canon pack** under `.claudinite/shared/` — a consumer improves only its own local packs.
- **Run on `opus`** — judging convertibility and authoring checks + fixtures is heavy judgment; this task declares `agent_model: opus`.

=== product-wiki RULES.md head ===
# product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki

This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki
under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in
place). Layout, required page sections, growth-log dating, source links,
staleness, and the isolation wall are **check-enforced** — the finding is the
instruction, so this prose never restates them. The full growth procedure is
the pack's task doc (`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`).

- **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never
  changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding
  that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and
  waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
  build on.
- **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before
  researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as
  open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass.
  Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current.
- **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A
  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source),
  never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's

# EdFringeNow — the data pipeline (scraper/ and data/)

The domain of this pack: getting show data out of edfringe.com and into the
committed files the site serves. Read it before touching `scraper/` or anything
under `data/`. The API's own field reference lives in
[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md) and the file layout in
[scraper/README.md](../../../../scraper/README.md) — this is the working
judgment those two don't carry.

## The live API is unreachable from a session — don't try, and don't fake it

`edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com` is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and
`edfringe.com` returns 403 to `WebFetch`. So: no session — this one included —
can verify a scraper change against live data. Anything that must touch the API
runs on a GitHub-hosted runner: the `Scrape edfringe shows (full)` workflow
(`.github/workflows/scrape.yml`), the `refresh-shows` / `refresh-tickets`
scheduled tasks, or the throwaway probe procedure in the `probe-edfringe-api`
skill. Never "verify" a scraper change by reasoning about what the API probably
returns — either run it on a runner, or say plainly that it is unverified.

`python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs
offline; it exercises raw→master→day-file→`shows.min.json` on a fixture, so a
normalizer change is verifiable here even though a fetch change is not. Because
it is the only offline verification a scraper change can get, it must stay wired
into `scripts/verify.sh` — the `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` check
enforces that (a step *label* naming the self-test does not count; only a command
line does).

## `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` boolean

"Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the
`soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to
sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and
`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available,
and unknown means available. Any new availability logic — client or scraper —
keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is carried through for display only.

The denylists that encode this live in two places (the Now page's
`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` and the planner's `UNAVAILABLE_STATUSES`), and losing
`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` from either renders those shows as buyable — so
the `edfringe-ticket-status-unavailable` check holds every such set in the
front-end code to both statuses. Whether the *judgment* is right for a new
status is still yours; that it does not silently regress is not.

## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it

`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.

## Changing the wire format is a four-file change

The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`, `p[].t`).
That encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:

- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
  `minify_master`)
- decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files
- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`

Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.

+`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
+`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
+fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
+`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
+full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
+`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.
+
+## Changing the wire format is a four-file change
+
+The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
+**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`, `p[].t`).
+That encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:
+
+- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
+  `minify_master`)
+- decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files
+- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
+  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
+  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`
+
+Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
+indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
+catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
+decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.

input.body:
Prose-to-checks sweep over this repo's own local packs (`.claudinite/local/packs/edfringe`, `.claudinite/local/packs/edfringe-data`).

Nothing outside `.claudinite/local/packs/edfringe-data/` is touched.

## `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` — blocking

**Prose it came from:** "*`python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs offline (it is a step in `scripts/verify.sh`).*"

The live edfringe API is unreachable from a session, so this self-test is the *only* offline verification a scraper change can get — drop it from the gate and normalizer changes ship with nothing standing in for it.

The check **strips `step "..."` labels and comments before looking**, because `verify.sh`'s own step heading quotes the command (`step "Normalizer self-test — normalize.py --selftest"`). A plain grep for the two tokens passes a script whose real invocation has been deleted; this one doesn't.

**See-it-fail:** confirmed red against mutated *real* repo content, not just fixtures — replacing the `verify.sh` invocation with an `echo` while leaving the step label in place turned `not ok - this repo's verify.sh still runs the normalizer self-test`; green again after revert. That's the mutation that matters, because it's exactly the case a grep-based check would wave through. The check also carries clean-input, relevance-first and false-alarm fixtures (commented-out invocations, trailing comments, no-normalizer trees).

## Withdrawn: `edfringe-ticket-status-unavailable`

The first revision of this PR also added a check holding every front-end availability denylist to `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` alongside `SOLD_OUT`. **That one has been removed** on owner correction: a pack rule is about *work procedures*, not product requirements, and "which shows the site treats as unavailable" is product behaviour. Being mechanically testable didn't make it pack-shaped.

The corpus already said so — `grow_with_claudinite/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md`:

> a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon or local, homes **how we work** […] A rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or that a feature's parts are wired to each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable spec and the suite that proves it.

The `ticketStatus` section of `edfringe-data/RULES.md` is restored to its prior wording.

⚠️ Removing that check leaves the two-status availability invariant with **no automated enforcement anywhere** — it was never covered by a product test. Its correct home is the executable spec this repo declares at `product/requirements.md`, which does not exist yet. Flagged for a separate call, not silently filled in here.

## Prose

Trimmed to rationale in `edfringe-data/RULES.md` — the *why* stays, the enforcement detail points at the check id. Nothing was deleted that a landed check doesn't now enforce.

## Verification

- `bash scripts/verify.sh` green — 142 tests pass, JS syntax, Python syntax, normalizer self-test.
- The new rule is confirmed loaded by the real pack registry (`loadPacks`), not just by the manifest assertion.
- No dangling references to the withdrawn check remain anywhere in the tree.

# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.
